title: YOU STOPPED READING ROMANS ONE VERSE TOO SOON
paragraphs: YOU STOPPED READING ROMANS ONE VERSE TOO SOON

Paul condemns sexual rebellion in Romans 1. Then, without giving the religious reader time to celebrate, he turns around and confronts the person holding the stones. Romans 1–2 is not merely somebody else’s indictment. It is a trapdoor beneath every self-righteous heart—and the only safe place left to fall is at the feet of Jesus.
There is a dangerous way to read Romans 1.
You can read every word Paul says about sexual sin…
and completely miss the moment when Paul turns around and starts talking to you.
That is what makes Romans 1–2 so uncomfortable.
Paul allows the morally confident reader to listen while humanity’s rebellion is exposed.
And somewhere in the middle of it, the religious person can begin feeling strangely comfortable.
“Finally somebody is willing to call sin what it is.”
One little Greek word changes the direction of the room.
Not “now let us begin an entirely different discussion.”
Paul has been building toward something.
And suddenly the person who thought he was sitting safely in the jury box discovers that Paul has called his name from the witness stand.
Διὸ ἀναπολόγητος εἶ, ὦ ἄνθρωπε πᾶς ὁ κρίνων
Dio anapologētos ei, ō anthrōpe pas ho krinōn.
“Therefore you are without excuse, O man, every one who judges.”
Because if Romans 1 has ever made you think primarily about “those people,” Romans 2 is coming for you.
Paul is not withdrawing what he has just said about sin.
He is destroying your ability to use what he said as a platform for self-righteous superiority.

Romans 1:26–27 really does contain strong language about same-sex sexual behavior. Paul writes of women exchanging what he calls the natural use for what is παρὰ φύσιν — para physin, “contrary to nature,” and of men leaving the natural sexual relation with women and burning in desire toward one another.
αἵ τε γὰρ θήλειαι αὐτῶν μετήλλαξαν τὴν φυσικὴν χρῆσιν εἰς τὴν παρὰ φύσιν
We should not make Paul say less than he says because his words make modern ears uncomfortable.
But neither should we make Romans say less than Romans says because the next words make religious ears uncomfortable.
Paul's argument does not end at Romans 1:27.
It does not even end at Romans 1:32.
The chapter number “2” was not written by Paul as a giant spiritual stop sign telling Christians, “You may now close the Bible and go condemn somebody.”
That may be one of the most important commands for anyone quoting Romans 1.
Because Paul is doing something devastating.
He first exposes humanity’s rejection of God.
Then he exposes the person who recognizes everyone else’s rebellion while remaining strangely blind to his own.
Romans 2 says your neighbor's sin does not make you righteous.
Some people want a Christianity that says, “Never judge anything. Sin is whatever you personally decide it is.”
Paul will not give us that Christianity.
Others want a Christianity that says, “Look how disgusting those sinners are. Thank God we aren't like them.”
Paul will not give us that Christianity either.
Truth without grace becomes a weapon in proud hands.
Grace without truth becomes permission to remain enslaved.
And power that begins transforming what grace has forgiven.
That is why Romans 2:1 is so frightening.
ἐν ᾧ γὰρ κρίνεις τὸν ἕτερον, σεαυτὸν κατακρίνεις
“For in that which you judge the other, you condemn yourself.”
There is a difference between recognizing that something is sinful and assuming that recognizing somebody else's sin somehow establishes your righteousness.
The Christian can say, “That is sin.”
But the Christian can never truthfully add:
Maybe your sexual history looks cleaner.
Maybe you never committed the sin you condemn most loudly.
What about the sins you learned to hide?
What about the bitterness nobody sees?
The pornography erased from the browser history?
The flirtation you insist “never became physical”?
The fantasies you entertain but would never confess?
The greed dressed up as ambition?
The gossip introduced with, “I'm only telling you so you can pray”?
The unforgiveness you have protected for fifteen years because the person who hurt you never apologized?
The worship song on your lips while resentment sits enthroned in your heart.
Be careful when somebody else's scandal makes you feel holy.
You may simply have found a sinner whose sins are easier for you to hate than your own.
And Paul knew exactly how to spring it.
Romans 1:18 begins with the wrath of God being revealed against human ungodliness and unrighteousness.
By Romans 2, Paul is confronting the judging person.
Everybody eventually finds himself standing beneath the same unbearable light.
Paul is not flattening every sin into identical earthly consequences.
Scripture does not require us to pretend every act produces exactly the same damage.
He is establishing something even more fundamental:
No category of sinner can manufacture righteousness by pointing at another category of sinner.
That is why Romans eventually arrives at the devastating conclusion:
“There is none righteous, no, not one.”
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
Romans is closing every escape route.
You walk inside carrying a folder containing everybody else's failures.
You know exactly what is wrong with the culture.
You know what is wrong with your neighbor.
You know what is wrong with that denomination.
You walk toward the Judge confident that your evidence will prove something about you.
You place the folder on His desk.
And asks the question you were hoping would never come.
Because the Gospel does not ask whether you can identify darkness.
It asks what you will do when God's light exposes yours.
This is where Romans 2 becomes astonishingly beautiful.
Because after confronting the judging heart, Paul says something many Christians can quote but sometimes fail to practice.
τὸ χρηστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ εἰς μετάνοιάν σε ἄγει
to chrēston tou theou eis metanoian se agei.
“The kindness of God leads you toward repentance.”
Not toward pretending sin does not matter.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia carries the idea of repentance, a change of mind and direction.
Grace is not God shrugging at our rebellion.
Grace is God meeting rebels with undeserved kindness and calling them home.
Repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is one of grace's miracles.
Jesus does not save us because our sins were insignificant.
He saves us because His mercy is greater.
The cross makes absolutely no sense if sin is trivial.
Why would the eternal Son of God enter our world, take flesh, suffer, bleed, and die if humanity merely needed encouragement?
The cross tells the truth about us.
And the cross tells an even greater truth about God.
He loved sinners enough to come for us anyway.
That means Romans 1 should never become ammunition for bullying gay people.
Nor should Romans 2 become ammunition for erasing what Romans 1 says about sexual morality.
We do not have to amputate one chapter to protect the other.
Homosexual sexual behavior is addressed as sin in Paul's argument.
Winning an argument about Romans cannot save you.
That is where the entire conversation must eventually go.
Not toward “Which group can we hate?”
Who will repent and come to Christ?
Maybe you are reading this and same-sex desire has been part of your struggle.
You are not beyond the reach of Jesus.
You are not beyond His reach.
Maybe you committed adultery and destroyed something you once promised God you would protect.
Maybe you slept with someone outside marriage last night.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been doing.
Maybe your sexual history is not your deepest shame at all.
And maybe you have spent years looking down at people whose sins look different from yours.
There is room at the foot of the cross for the sexually broken person.
There is room for the hypocrite.
There is room for the religious fraud.
There is room for the ashamed.
There is room for the person who knew better.
There is room for the person who promised, “Never again,” and then did it again.
But nobody walks through the door carrying a résumé proving why he deserved admission.
And this is where the scandal becomes grace.
The scandal is not merely that sinners sinned.
The scandal is that the holy God moved toward guilty people.
The scandal is that Christ died for the ungodly.
The scandal is that the cross has room for people we would have cancelled forever.
The scandal is that Jesus can take the person whose history seems permanently attached to his name and give him another identity.
Not because sin suddenly became acceptable.
Because Christ paid for sin and broke its claim upon those who belong to Him.
“Good people, congratulations. You correctly identified the bad people.”
And once you understand that, it becomes harder to throw stones.
You can still call sin sin.
You can still hold biblical convictions.
You can still refuse to celebrate what Scripture forbids.
But you cannot stand beneath a blood-stained cross bragging about your superiority.
The Man hanging there is innocent.
That changes the tone of everything.
We don't approach sinners as people who never needed rescue.
We approach them as beggars who found Bread.
We don't say, “Become like us and perhaps God will tolerate you.”
“Come meet the Savior who confronted our sin, carried our guilt, forgave our rebellion, and is still changing us.”
Grace without pretending repentance is unnecessary.
And repentance without believing your worst chapter gets the final word.
Maybe this article made you uncomfortable.
It was never written merely to provide ammunition for arguments.
It was written as part of an apostolic proclamation of the Gospel that strips human beings of boasting and drives sinners toward the righteousness God provides.
So before you share Romans 1 against somebody else, read Romans 2 over yourself.
Keep going until Romans 3 closes your mouth.
Keep going until Romans 5 shows Christ dying for the ungodly.
Keep going until Romans 6 tells you grace is not permission to continue comfortably in sin.
Keep going until Romans 8 announces that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Keep going until the question stops being:
The sexually pure but unbearably proud churchgoer needs Jesus.
The person writing this needs Jesus.
The person reading it needs Jesus.
There are no spectators at Calvary.
So if this exposed something you have hidden behind religious respectability, don't perform for the comments.
Not because typing a sentence saves anyone.
But sometimes confession begins when pride finally stops pretending.
Send it privately to the person who thinks Christians only know how to condemn.
Send it to the believer who has confused biblical conviction with spiritual superiority.
Send it to the struggling Christian who needs to remember that repentance still has a door—and that door has not been nailed shut.
Because there will come a day when somebody quotes Romans 1 as though Romans 2 never happened, or Romans 2 as though Romans 1 suddenly disappeared.
Come back and read them together.
This ministry exists to keep putting Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ in front of people who desperately need it.
If you want to help us glorify God through the continued spread of His Word, this is one practical way you can stand with the mission:
And there is something else we want believers to know.

And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because there are moments when another believer needs to see that they are not the only one being convicted, fighting temptation, repenting, healing, and learning to live beneath grace.
That may be the testimony somebody else desperately needed tonight.
Because Romans 1 was never permission to hate the sinner.
Romans 2 was never permission to redefine sin.
And the Gospel was never permission for any of us to pretend we did not need the cross.
The finger you pointed at someone else's scandal may be the very thing God uses to lead your eyes back to your own need for grace.
And when you finally have nothing left to prove…
The Judge who knows your whole story is the Savior who gave His life to redeem sinners—and your worst chapter does not have to be the last chapter when Jesus holds the pen.
